questions.stem: During the cardiac cycle, the atria contract before the ventricles. Why is this sequence important?

options.text: Atrial contraction generates higher pressure than ventricular contraction
Atrial contraction pushes blood into the ventricles, filling them before the ventricles contract to pump blood out of the heart
The atria need to rest while the ventricles work
The atria contract to close the semilunar valves

questions.explanation: The atria contract first to push blood down into the ventricles through the open atrioventricular valves, filling them completely. The ventricles then contract with much greater force to push blood out through the arteries. If both contracted simultaneously, the ventricles would not be fully filled and would pump less blood per beat.

questions.stem: The SAN (sinoatrial node) is often called the heart's natural pacemaker. It is located in the right atrium. What does it do?

options.text: It produces hormones that control heart rate
It generates electrical impulses that cause the atria to contract, setting the rhythm of the heartbeat
It pumps blood from the right atrium to the right ventricle
It prevents blood from flowing backwards

questions.explanation: The SAN is a small group of specialised cells that spontaneously generate electrical impulses at regular intervals. These impulses spread across both atria, causing them to contract. The impulse then reaches the AVN (atrioventricular node), which delays it slightly before sending it to the ventricles, ensuring the correct contraction sequence.

questions.stem: A patient has a faulty SAN that generates impulses too slowly. Their resting heart rate is only 35 beats per minute. What treatment would a doctor recommend?

options.text: Surgery to remove the SAN
Implanting an artificial pacemaker that generates regular electrical impulses
Prescribing caffeine tablets permanently
A heart transplant

questions.explanation: An artificial pacemaker is a small electronic device implanted under the skin that sends electrical impulses to the heart to maintain a normal rhythm. It takes over the function of the faulty SAN, ensuring the heart beats at an appropriate rate. This is a common and effective treatment for bradycardia (slow heart rate).

questions.stem: During vigorous exercise, heart rate increases from 70 to 150 beats per minute. Which part of the nervous system controls this increase?

options.text: The somatic (voluntary) nervous system
The autonomic nervous system, via hormones like adrenaline and nerve signals to the SAN
The central nervous system directly contracts the heart
The heart rate is controlled by the lungs

questions.explanation: Heart rate is controlled involuntarily by the autonomic nervous system. During exercise, the hormone adrenaline is released by the adrenal glands, and sympathetic nerve impulses increase the rate at which the SAN fires. This increases heart rate, delivering more oxygen and glucose to exercising muscles. You cannot consciously control your heart rate.

questions.stem: A pressure graph of the cardiac cycle shows a sharp rise in ventricular pressure. At the point where ventricular pressure exceeds atrial pressure, what happens to the atrioventricular valves?

options.text: They open, allowing blood to flow from atria to ventricles
They close, preventing blood from flowing back into the atria
They remain open throughout the cardiac cycle
They vibrate to produce the heartbeat sound

questions.explanation: When the ventricles begin to contract, pressure in the ventricles rises. Once ventricular pressure exceeds atrial pressure, the atrioventricular valves snap shut to prevent backflow of blood into the atria. This closure produces the first heart sound ('lub'). The semilunar valves then open when ventricular pressure exceeds arterial pressure.
